Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. The energy-driven evolution of these patterns may reflect the role of cosmic magnetic fields in disrupting cosmic distributions over time, while the widespread alignment with the Supergalactic Plane suggests a significant influence of the galactic distribution on itself. We conclude by emphasizing the need for higher sensitivity experiments to thoroughly explore the nature of these patterns and the vast universe that generates them. The complex structure of these patterns is also accessible for experiments like the Auger Next Generation, and the Giant Radio Array for New Gravitational Wave Observatories, through a higher sensitivity and a radio extension, respectively. The energetic dependence observed in the laboratory for extremely energetic cosmic anisotropies may be particularly useful for future experiments once the energy range of these experiments is raised above 4 EeV. This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in relational tables that contain missing values and functional dependencies. Unlike traditional approaches that assume a rigid schema, our method enables flexibility with optional attributes, treated as functional dependencies that may not always hold. We've developed a framework to handle inconsistent tables with nulls and functional dependencies, categorizing inconsistencies into three types: between values, between attributes, and between tuples. Our approach applies repair methods and consistency maintaining operations to handle these differences, ensuring consistency with optional attributes and foreign-like constraints. We've also established a hierarchy of our specific repair strategies within the framework of general approaches, such as applying actions to transform the table or determining the degree of inconsistency. Furthermore, we've established conditions under which different repair strategies produce the same outcome, such as when the inconsistency involves a repeated value or when one value is missing in relation to another. Moreover, we've explored extending our framework to handle embedded queries and evaluated our approach using real-world datasets, demonstrating that our method effectively and efficiently handles inconsistencies with foreign-like constraints and missing values. We believe this research contributes significantly to the existing body of knowledge on inconsistent data, particularly in the context of tables with nulls and functional dependencies. The findings presented in this research have been applied to develop an algorithm that can determine the degree of inconsistency in tables with null values and functional dependencies, as well as an evaluation of this algorithm against publicly available datasets available for testing relational join algorithms. The research also explores the relationship between repair strategies and consistency maintaining operations, as well as the concept of equivalence between different repair strategies, such as replacing one value with another, or replacing one value with null, or removing one value in relation to another value. The research further examines the issue of evaluating queries over tables with null values and functional dependencies, including the evaluation of embedded queries, as well as the evaluation of the degree of inconsistency in tables with null values and foreign-like constraints, demonstrated using real-world datasets. This study presents an innovative approach to modeling time-dependent patterns in data, specifically focusing on applications in economics, demography, and biology. Our research addresses a critical challenge posed by time series data, namely the absence of a universal method to handle both non-stationary behavior and structural changes. To tackle this issue, we combine two established techniques: the Poisson autoregressive model and the linear state-space time series framework. By integrating these methods, we derive mathematical formulas to estimate parameters using the expectation-maximization algorithm and the Kalman filter, which provide a solid foundation for analyzing and understanding our proposed model. To demonstrate the practical utility of our model, we also outline a step-by-step procedure for predicting future observations. To validate our model, we conduct a comprehensive set of tests, comparing it to alternative methods using real data generated in a simulation study and actual datasets in economics, demography, and biology. These datasets include counts of stock prices, COVID-19 cases and fatalities, and species populations, among others. Our results show that the model excels in capturing complex patterns and performs well even in the presence of significant structural changes, although there is scope for improvement in addressing extreme events and non-count data. Our model has the potential to be valuable for any application involving the analysis of counts over time. To facilitate further development, we highlight a set of potential research directions, including the integration of other state space models, the development of forecasting tools, and the creation of R software for implementing the model. To conclude, this study offers a novel perspective on modeling time-dependent patterns in data and provides a framework for researchers to build upon in further advancing the model. Our proposed Neural Descriptor Fields construct object representations that
incorporate local, precise measurements and demonstrate high levels of
robustness in various scenarios, including partial views, external lighting
variations, and rotations, while requiring a single training image per object.
These representations maintain their accuracy when combining objects and
rotating/mirroring them, exhibiting perfect invariants under 3D SE(3) transformations.
For the task of object combination, our representations achieve a 90% success
rate at the most challenging condition (20% occlusion), surpassing the state
art with a 10% margin.
However, a significant limitation in our current setup is the lack of a
true neural network-based object generator, leading to suboptimal performance
in more complex object combination scenarios.
We believe that our Neural Descriptor Fields have vast potential for other
object processing tasks, such as removal and insertion, as well as for
explicit object generation techniques.
We demonstrate this potential by integrating our Neural Descriptor Fields
with a non-neural object removal technique, resulting in outstanding
performance in difficult scenarios. Our framework and evaluations are available
at https://neuraldescriptorfields.org/.

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through clustering of projection points, regardless of whether a 2D-2D correspondence problem is formulated to estimate pose in the second stage. This study introduces the concept of projection point clustering to demonstrate that, alternatively, a comparison problem between 2D projections can be formulated instead. This comparison problem is equivalent to determining the object-axis axis intersection, and its solution yields the 6D object pose. Experimentation using the BOP Dataset demonstrates our approach yields higher accuracy than the current state-of-the-art, especially in situations with low-resolution images. Numerous molecular dynamics simulations integrate configurational gradients from force fields to advance to the next time step. For our purpose in constructing an automated sampling framework for molecular configurations, we designed a new dynamical model that relies on forces to guide the simulation. Our model takes the form of Langevin dynamics, allowing for efficient sampling of molecular configurations by exploring local minima in energy landscapes. To further enhance our simulator's performance, we developed an adaptive step-size method that ensures simulation stability and optimizes computational efficiency. Our results demonstrate that this dynamical model yields superior configurational samples compared to alternative methods, even when utilizing relatively brief simulation periods. We exploit our simulator's unique ability to explore local energy landscapes to discover initial configurational guesses that yield significantly better maximum a posteriori errors than random initial conditions. To facilitate seamless integration into existing optimization frameworks, we show that our simulator can be operated in a dynamical NVE mode that replicates the same thermodynamic conditions as its initial configurational distribution. Our code is called MolDyn, and it is available for public use. Our approach and code can be applied to a broad range of molecular sampling applications, including chemistry-based game decision-making and the initial stages of molecular optimization tasks. Our further development of MolDyn includes expanding the simulator to handle bond formation and breaking, which significantly enhances its capabilities to explore complex and diverse molecular configurations that vary in size. To this end, we introduce a new dynamic simulator module called MolDyn-HD, capable of efficiently track and change bond lengths during simulations. As its name suggests, MolDyn-HD is particularly effective at efficiently handle large molecular habitats that comprise diverse and complex distributions of molecules. Our MolDyn-HD simulator includes a specialized version of the Hamiltonian dynamics simulator, which we call Hamiltonian Dynamic Tracker (HDT), designed to track and change configurational variables such as bond lengths during simulations. To further enhance simulation performance and reduce HDT-induced errors, we developed a hybrid tracker called HDT-HH, which uses two different trackers, one simple and precise, and one complex and efficient, and switches between them based on simulation progress. Our results demonstrate that HDT-HH tracker reduces simulation-induced errors and enhances performance compared to alternative methods. corresponds to a de Sitter space. In this study, we formulate the Dirac equation within 
$R$-Minkowski space and establish that it is analogous to the Dirac equation defined

equation within $R$-Minkowski space can be interpreted through a complex geometric 
framework by introducing a de Sitter space geometry. We then determine the fundamental 
operators of the algebra $sp(4,R)$, which form the complex geometric structure of 
which the Dirac equation within $R$-Minkowski space is composed. We then determine 
the conserved current operators using both the Poisson bracket method and the complex 
geometric structure method. We demonstrate that both methods yield identical results.

Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a quicker and more efficient approach using alone CT scans for accurately identifying tumors in the esophagus. A novel deep learning model called Dense Focus Unet (DFUnet) is introduced, which produces detailed mappings from any input image. By incorporating a unique dense transfer block, DFUnet allows for precise control over the scope of these mappings, thereby enabling the development of a successful tumor segmentation algorithm. Experimental results show that this model can be highly effective in isolating tumors from CT scans of the esophagus, with a score of 87% in comparison with a conventional baseline method. Code-mixed languages encompass the synergetic result of bilingual speakers combining words from two different languages within a single utterance, such as "I am going to Delhi via Chandigarh" in Hindi-English. This communication method is particularly prevalent in social media platforms and offers valuable information, in contrast to monolingual data. Code-mixed data offers several advantages, including, but not limited to, eliminating language barriers and providing more comprehensive knowledge. Nevertheless, developers face a major hurdle in incorporating code-mixed data due to its complex nature, given the intricacies of modeling multiple languages simultaneously. This issue is further compounded by the challenge of establishing a common framework for evaluation and comparison. Additionally, both statistical and rule-based approaches exhibit significant limitations in their ability to handle code-mixed data. In the context of NLP tasks, several issues arise, such as defining appropriate evaluation metrics, establishing a standard protocol for data pre-processing, and developing reliable models that can generalize across different languages. In order to break down these barriers, this paper invites submissions that demonstrate viable solutions to these problems, with the ultimate goal of establishing a community that can collaborate and address these challenges in code-mixed NLP.

Quantifying the quality of automatic image descriptions is crucial, and one widely used method is comparing them to human-generated descriptions. Although this approach is straightforward, it assumes that current description generation techniques are comparable to human performance. This paper disputes this assumption by presenting two findings. First, it shows that human descriptions vary significantly when different people describe the same image, a phenomenon we call the "inter-annotator description diversity issue." To measure this diversity, the authors develop a method that calculates the quality of a single description in the context of a given distribution of other possible descriptions. Second, the authors discover that benchmark data currently used to evaluate automatic image description generation systems suffers from low diversity, which can lead to flawed evaluations. In particular, systems that simply repeat the same description across different images are inadvertently rewarded with high scores. To address these issues, the authors suggest using selective benchmarks that prioritize diversity for evaluating human-generated data and floating evaluation distributions to make automatic systems more adaptable to the variety of images and descriptions. The proposed approaches are demonstrated to improve the quality of automatic systems at describing both simple and complex images. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances. This paper also introduces a method for comparing utterances, and outlines a strategy for validating system behavior. Furthermore, we outline a simple example illustrating the application of this strategy. This work has been incorporated into the structure of a larger PhD research project. The associated code is available for public use at https://github.com/AmirHosseinK/ConverseTest. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target domain recommendation approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel concept, multi-sparse-domain (MSD) recommendation, which assumes multiple sparse domains are present. We then propose a novel MS-Domain recommendation framework, termed Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation via Enhanced Comprehensive Aspect Preference Learning (MDCAPEAR). This framework leverages an advanced, multi-domain comprehensive aspect preference learning model to effectively explore inter-domain and intra-domain connections by incorporating a unique, multi-domain comprehensive aspect preference learning model where domain-agnostic and domain-specific preferences are learned in an integrated manner. This model enables a rich, complex representation of user preferences across multiple sparse domains. To further enhance the representation, we introduce a memory-based intra-domain injection mechanism that allows for the flexible incorporation of intra-domain information to enhance the representation of user specific comprehensive aspect preferences. Furthermore, we propose a multi-domain adaptive strategy for balancing inter-domain and intra-domain adaptation, which ensures seamless integration of the model, infrastructure, and data across multiple sparse domains without additional supervision. The proposed MDCAPEAR framework is computationally efficient and can be scalable to real-world large-scale datasets. We conduct extensive experiments on five real-world datasets and the results demonstrate the superiority of MDCAPEAR in addressing multi-sparse-domain recommendation tasks in various settings. The proposed approach is available at https://github.com/{github-handle}/MDCAPEAR. The code has been optimized for scalability and is suitable for large-scale datasets. The proposed framework provides practical implications for the successful deployment of real-world recommender systems in various settings and can be applied across multiple areas including but not limited to online advertising, movie recommendation, and e-commerce. The solution to a conic equation is a concept fundamental to convex optimization, defined as the smallest set satisfying a given set of convex inequalities. This paper introduces a novel approach where the solution to conic equations is treated as a natural cone, thereby enabling their use in dual problems. A particular example of such a natural cone is shown to have an intuitive interpretation in a linear regression problem. Furthermore, this paper demonstrates the application of these natural cones in solving a linear regression problem with an $\ell_1$-regularized objective and robust stability criteria. A Julia package, Hypatia.Jl, is also introduced to provide an easy-to-use interface for defining and working with these natural cones. Although Hypatia.Jl is currently limited to dual conversion and does not support direct conversion, it does support complex, nested conic equations and provides an interactive visualization of the solution cone. Despite its limited capabilities, Hypatia.Jl has been successfully used to solve large-scale data science problems, one of which involves a linear regression task with multiple factors. The code for Hypatia.Jl is open-source and available on GitHub, contributing to the broader optimization community a valuable tool with practical utility. The approach of treating the solution to conic equations as natural cones provides researchers with a new paradigm, presenting opportunities for further exploration and development. The code for Hypatia.Jl, along with example datasets for the linear regression problems solved using this package, is appended to this paper as the Supplement. The package is also freely downloadable from www.hypatia.jl. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality assessment to ensure rapid and accurate analysis, especially for extensive research projects. MRI data quality evaluation is a multi-classification task, involving multiple factors such as noise, artifacts, and irregularities, that are frequently evaluated by experts on a scale of 1 to 5. To enhance the efficiency of this process, machine learning models are being explored to automate quality assessment, either by analyzing input data alone or with the assistance of limited expert input. However, the effectiveness of these models relies on massive amounts of labeled data, which are difficult and time-consuming to prepare due to their detailed nature. This study presents a novel approach to train MRI quality assessment models using a single label, either 1 or 5, which significantly reduces the data preparation time and increases model robustness to provide more accurate results. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, we conducted two experiments: one on phantom data and another on actual brain MRI data from multiple scanners. In both cases, we evaluated our approach against the traditional method of training models with detailed labels, which necessitate extensive expert input. Our results show that the proposed method of using single labels yields comparable, and in some cases better, results compared to the traditional method of using detailed labels, which is reflected in its lower generalization error and higher F1-score scores. Our research offers a scalable and efficient framework for MRI data quality assessment that can be conveniently implemented in various applications. Moreover, our findings are available as an MRI quality assessment notebook, which is accessible on GitHub. This notebook provides an interactive environment to train, evaluate, and visualize various MRI quality assessment models, along with an interface to excel-like spreadsheets for data and model analysis. This notebook can be utilized by researchers to evaluate the effectiveness of various MRI quality assessment models and develop new ones, which is reflected in its nomination for best paper award at the IEEE BRITAIN 2023 conference. To understand how private electric vehicles influence the resilience of distribution networks, we developed a decision-making framework for optimal charging and driving paths utilizing a mix of robust optimization and multi-agent theory. A key aspect of this approach involves defining pricing strategies by the grid operator to manage network stability and identify resilient configurations, while also considering the interconnectedness of transportation and energy systems. To evaluate the impacts of private EVs on distribution network resilience, our framework enables the analysis of various scenarios, comparing the effects of different pricing policies, transportation infrastructure, and private EV behaviors on the network's resilience. Furthermore, this research provides a practical solution for grid operators to implement effective pricing strategies that prioritize network stability and offer convenient travel options for private EV users. To support this, we include numerical examples based on a case study in the city of Suzhou, China. This study demonstrates how optimized pricing can reduce the risk of network disruption and lower the costs of private EV charging by improving route planning and consolidating nearby private EV registrations into larger transportation hubs. The results show that a relatively simple pricing approach, the Concentration Discount Policy, can significantly enhance network resilience and overall efficiency. The findings of this research can be applied to other urban settings with similar transportation and energy systems. To facilitate replication, the code used for this research is publicly available. This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials crystallizing in the AuCu3 structure. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 compound and indicate that CmSn3 and GdSn3 both adopt a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and display metallic behavior. Notably, the magnetic moment diminishes with rising Cm content in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, and these materials share some key characteristics, rendering them promising for spintronic technology applications. Furthermore, we explored the series for potential phase segregation into GdSn3 and CmSn3 phases using the generalized pseudopotential approach and found that both scenarios are feasible, depending on the x value. Lastly, we discussed possible synthesis pathways for these compounds and proposed that they can be grown using molecular beam epitaxy or pulsed laser deposition techniques. Lastly, we suggested possible experiments, including specific heat and magnetization measurements, and molecular dynamics simulations to better understand the behavioral changes occurring within the GdxCm1-xSn3 series.

The paper discusses expected findings from experiments at the RHIC and LHC, focusing on predictions for new baryon and meson particles that may be discovered. A range of models, including chiral bag models, quark combination models, and gauge theory at high temperatures, anticipate the presence of additional hadrons that could be identified through experiments at next-generation colliders. A comprehensive list of predicted hadrons is presented, ranging from strange baryons and mesons to exotic particles composed of glues and quarks, as well as those made of heavy quarks. The predicted particles have mass estimates based on various models, and are categorized by quark composition to facilitate identification. The authors suggest that discovery of these predicted hadrons will rely heavily on advanced computational tools that utilize lattice QCD, combine data from different experiments, and involve complex statistical analysis. The paper also explores potential findings of hadron particles predicted by spin-3 baryon models that may resemble known particles once the underlying physics is understood. The list of predicted hadrons includes 13 baryons and 16 mesons, in addition to 5 exotic hadrons composed of heavy quarks, with mass estimates ranging from a few GeV to over 100 GeV, and predictions that some of these hadrons may exist in stable forms. The authors further speculate that discoveries at next-generation colliders may lead to a better comprehension of physics beyond the Standard Model. The Coxeter group foundation theorem, initially proven by Bouscaren and Reutenauer, essentially states that a free group is generated by the elements of a Coxeter group if and only if its characteristic subgroup, defined by the product of its odd powers, is trivial. In this paper, we generalize this result for the B-type Coxeter groups by demonstrating that there is a close relationship between the structure of a Coxeter group of type B and its associated free group. Specifically, we demonstrate that a Coxeter group of type B is generated by the set of its elements if and only if its natural presentation in the free group includes a specific property, equivalent to the absence of certain odd cycles. Additionally, we establish that the group's structure is preserved when considering the derived series of the free group. Moreover, we provide a straightforward criterion to determine if the group's structure is preserved when considering the lower central series of the free group. Both of these conditions can be difficult to assess directly, but we show that they can also be determined by examining the element's distribution within the group's matrix diagram. Furthermore, we establish that the presence of an odd cycle in the matrix diagram is synonymous with the presence of a specific cycle in the lower central series, which can be determined using the Kostka matrix to predict the outcome for an arbitrary distribution of elements. Finally, we include a concise appendix detailing the Kostka matrix, the cycle structure, and the relationship between the B-type Coxeter group's free presentation and its defining relations. This information may also be useful to researchers studying the underlying subject matter.

We've developed a method to estimate weak lensing effects on Type Ia Supernovae using the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and the DES Y3 weak lensing field convergence maps. By applying a Bayesian approach and taking into account systematic errors, we calculated the average weak lensing magnification experienced by each SN Ia observation. This resulted in a well-defined distribution for the average magnification of each SN Ia, which we calculated as $1.37 \pm 0.09$, and this matches our independent estimation using a different method. Furthermore, we found that this approach can be used to remove the weak lensing signal from SN Ia data, with an resolution that can be improved by using higher-resolution lensing maps in the future. Leveraging this capability, we removed an estimated $2.4 \pm 0.1$ per cent from the SN Ia distance ratio uncertainty in the Pantheon dataset. This is a crucial consideration for current and future SN Ia datasets, which will be increasingly influenced by lensing deflection and the abundance of lensing targets within their fields of view. Understanding this effect is crucial for placing higher limits on the Hubble constant and for detecting the acceleration of the cosmic expansion. Understanding and calculating this effect on SN Ia data is also vital for correctly interpreting future observations driven by the cosmic lensing foreground, such as the Square Kilometre Array and the Euclid SN focus. This approach can be applied to any SN Ia dataset based on observed fields, without the need for additional information. Despite being independent of the DES Y3 team, our estimation of the average magnification experienced by the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and the DES Y3 weak lensing field convergence maps is consistent with the DES Y3 result of $1.47 \pm 0.06$. This result highlights the similarity between the SN Ia selection function and the weak lensing shear selection function, which could be further explored in the future. This approach opens up new possibilities for removing the lensing signal from SN Ia data based on the shear correlation function, which could place higher limits on the Hubble constant and detect the acceleration of the cosmic expansion in future SN Ia datasets. This could also drive the focus of future surveys, such as the Euclid SN focus, to reduce the lensing contamination of SN Ia data by increasing the angular separation between SN Ia observations. This research introduces a novel concept, T nodes, which are basic structures composed of two T pieces that can be combined to create more complex designs, particularly useful for implementing inner working elements in free-space optical interconnects. We demonstrate the functional integration of T nodes with 2x2 multi-mode couplers in a silicon-on-insulator material, leveraging mode field engineering to achieve high channel crosstalk tolerance. Our findings also reveal that these T nodes can be efficiently linked to couplers through a 2-D micro-assembler, while maintaining precision and reducing the risk of defects. Moreover, we experimentally verify the effective operation of T nodes within a 16x16 optical interconnect, showcasing its potential in complex optical systems. The widespread application of T nodes in optical systems could be made possible by creating a library of pre-fabricated T pieces, enabling the flexible and efficient construction of complex optical elements. The material and fabrication methods presented in this study are specifically designed for silicon-on-insulator material, although the T nodes could be adapted to suit other materials. The T pieces can be combined in various ways to create diverse optical elements, including those with loop, fork, and ring structures, among others. This paper introduces the concept of a symplectic transformation known as conversion, which transforms a given symplectic transformation into an equivalent form with reversed parity. We demonstrate that any conformally smooth symplectic transformation is generically susceptible to a series of successive conversions, ultimately leading to a deterministic outcome of either localization, splitting, or conformal equivalence. The analysis involves a systematic examination of the critical curve associated with conversion, as well as the development of new renormalization group methods that introduce conversion fixed points and the associated critical behavior. These results expand on previous studies by providing a comprehensive, group-theoretic analysis of conformal classes under the symplectic conjugation group, and revealing that the dynamics of conversion can be unified with the dynamics of splitting and localization through the application of group theoretical tools. Specifically, we identify a invariant known as the conversion parity, which serves as a distinguishing factor for each dynamics mode. Furthermore, the introduction of a new inner metric allows us to apply inner classical Hodge theory directly to conformal currents, thereby gaining access to the properties of conformal currents and the dynamics of conversion parity. The study of conversion parity dynamics sheds new light on the properties of symplectic rephrasing, splitting, localization, and Kummer bound states, and reveals that certain states, such as localized states or splitting states, exhibit specific parity properties that dictate their transformation under symplectic rephrasing. Conversely, we demonstrate that the dynamics of conversion parity also serves as a necessary condition for a symplectic state to be resistant to splitting or localization, or to exhibit Kummer properties. The paper at its conclusion presents an open problem related to the dynamics of conversion parity in the context of monodromy groups. The associated calculations are organized into three parts, with the first part examining conversion parity and its dynamics in the absence of boundary contributions. The second part explores the relationship between the inner metric and the normal bundle, with the third part analyzing the local properties of conversion parity dynamics. The paper also includes three appendices that provide additional mathematical context. The primary stars associated with this submission are for the work described in sections 2, 3, and 4, with the secondary stars for the results presented in sections 5, 6, and 7. The paper closes with a brief discussion in section 7 and three appendices A, B, and C. The results presented in this paper were previously published in the arXiv archive. A key challenge in modern organ transplantation involves managing the large pool of unused kidney donations. A notable issue arises when a patient's immunological profile doesn't match any available donor kidneys, making their transplants high-risk. Currently, patients with poor match profiles are often excluded from receiving transplants. However, recent advances in immunosuppression techniques have significantly reduced the dangers of such transplants. Given this development, it's now beneficial to consider incorporating these patients into the transplant system. In this work, we aim to optimize the allocation of kidneys to patients with poor match profiles. By leveraging recent advancements in immunosuppression, we can now safely transplant patients with increasingly marginal match profiles. Unfortunately, there are more patients in need of transplants than available kidneys. As a result, a waiting list has formed, and kidneys are often rejected due to poor match profiles. To tackle this issue, we can use priority systems to give higher preference to patients with better match profiles. On the other hand, another approach involves using economic methods to value each kidney donation based on how well it matches a patient. In this work, we focus on the latter approach and use mathematical modeling to describe the distribution of kidney donations and patients' immunological profiles. We then formulate an optimal acceptance policy to minimize waste and waittime by evaluating the financial and biological value of each kidney donation. By combining queue theory and stochastic control methods, we develop a solution to this complex problem. Although this model is too complex to solve numerically, it serves as a valuable theoretical framework. To overcome this limitation, we develop a simplified model that can be solved using numerical methods. Both models yield comparable results, demonstrating their practical utility. To further validate our approach, we conduct a series of simulation experiments using realistic data. These experiments involve varying model parameters, adding noise to estimates, and altering patients' and donors' characteristics. We find that our optimal policy consistently reduces waste and waittime across these scenarios. In addition to organ transplantation, our model also has applications in other contexts where resources must be allocated to agents with varying levels of compatibility. In such scenarios, our model can be adapted to maximize compatibility while accounting for additional factors like spatial distance between agents and the location of available resources. In conclusion, this work addresses a significant challenge in modern organ transplantation and provides a mathematical framework for allocating kidneys to patients based on their immunological profile. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. Our work also explores different model variants and provides a mathematical framework for the analysis of these models, offering a versatile toolset for the theoretical examination of NLP embeddings along with guidance on interpreting and selecting the appropriate model, including the selection of hyperparameters. We conclude that the word2vec model is an outstanding tool for capturing frequentist synonyms but requires caution when relying on its embeddings of polarized words or company names due to its tendency to confuse antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Our analysis of time-varying patterns also opens up new research possibilities in the field of financial natural language processing. This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IDEA systems as alternatives to our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1].
Fair through line-of-sight obstructions and rich scattering environments, IDEA systems utilize data and radio frequency (RF) power at different frequencies to generate an additional gain beyond the benefits provided by multiple antennas and multiple carriers.
In [1], we demonstrated that such a scheme leads to a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) gain of $10 \log_{10} (4) \approx 6$ dB for a system with four antennas and four carriers.
For scattering channel conditions, we determined the average ideal frequency pairs that maximize the SC-RF-SNR for SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems.
We also defined a binary phase shift keying (BPSK)-OFDM waveforming strategy as a specific case of SISO-OFDM, which results in an average SC-RF-SNR gain of $10 \log_{10} (3.18) \approx 4.7$ dB.
Furthermore, we investigated the average IDEA-SNR and found that it converges to the average IDEA-SNR gain, which is less sensitive to changes in the number of antennas and carriers.
We explored various scattering channel models and confirmed the simplicity of BPSK-OFDM, which is applicable in a wide range of scenarios.
Finally, we simulated an IDEA-BPSK-OFDM system in a scenario with a base station and mobile devices and demonstrated the effectiveness of this scheme.

This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries. Furthermore, we've compared our results to established literature, demonstrating close agreement and improving the resolution of certain scenarios. To accommodate dynamic boundary conditions, we've introduced a numerical predictor--corrector technique to determine the precise location of changing phase boundaries. In addition, we've explored two different approaches to implement the level-set function within the embedded boundary framework and discussed their respective advantages and limitations. To facilitate the implementation of this method for practical purposes, we've made the source code available openly. This study has also highlighted potential areas for improvement, such as optimizing the numerical predictor--corrector technique and implementing better methods to handle phase changes, which could further enhance this model. Overall, our research has demonstrated that this combined level-set and embedded boundary approach provides a versatile and highly effective numerical tool for modeling complex phenomena involving changing phase boundaries. This approach has been applied to a range of scenarios in physics and biology, including solidification, melting, and pattern formation, and could also be used to model similar processes in other fields, such as geochemistry and astrophysics. This approach has further been compared to alternative methods based on front-tracking and Navier--Stokes CFD, which are more resource-intensive but can handle more complex scenarios, and could be used in combination with this combined level-set and embedded boundary approach in inhomogeneous domains. This research has also highlighted the importance of resolving the resolution of the changing phase boundaries for low resolution simulations, which could be achieved by using higher resolution grids or more advanced numerical schemes, such as fourth-order conservative numerical schemes, and could be used to guide the implementation of this model in practical applications. This study has further been applied to explore the dynamics of melting boundaries in an expanding domain, which could be used as a model for certain natural phenomena, such as the formation of basalt columns, and has also been used to model the growth of dendrites, which could be used as a model for certain technological applications, such as the development of solidification patterns in liquid metals, and could also be used to model the formation of ice crystals

In multiagent systems, an equilibrium is a stable state where agents adhere to their strategies, assuming all other agents behave similarly. Despite the significance of identifying equilibria for real-world applications, including market competition and traffic patterns, there's a major obstacle: the lack of meaningful interpretation underlying traditional equilibrium learning methods. This limitation becomes particularly challenging when working with complex, modern datasets that often utilize deep neural networks. To address this issue, our research focuses on developing a method to make deep multiagent equilibrium learning both transparent and feasible by incorporating feature attribution techniques that enable the interpretation of learned equilibria. Furthermore, we introduce a new evaluation metric that assesses the closeness of a learned state to an equilibrium while considering the underlying incentives that agents should be attempting to maximize. This approach enables the seamless integration of feature attribution techniques and the evaluation of the closeness of a learned state to an equilibrium, thereby providing a comprehensive framework for deep multiagent equilibrium learning. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on a range of multiagent learning tasks, including those with simple and complex networks, and show that it outperforms traditional evaluation methods for evaluating the closeness of a learned state to an equilibrium. Our code is available at https://github.com/xiangyi108/DeepExEQ. This work was presented at the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems. This notion can be extended to multiple SLEs, with multiple Gaussian free fields acting as sources. In the case of a single SLE, the associated Gaussian free field must have zero boundary hysteresis due to topological reasons. However, for SLEs with multiple components, there are multiple Gaussian free fields, each with the ability to create a separate curve. The interaction between these curves and the associated Gaussian free fields can be understood through the statistic of boundary hysteresis. The law of the Gaussian free field is determined by the random point process $\mu_t$ through the statistic of boundary hysteresis, which serves as a source for the SLE. Understanding how genomic function affects association with specific traits is a key goal in genetics research. We developed a method to integrate both types of information across the genome and ranked regions of the genome by their association with 18 different human traits. We discovered that certain traits, such as blood traits, tend to involve elements like promoter regions and those near gene start sites. The LHC is an versatile accelerator that can produce a wide range of secondary particles, both through nucleon-nucleus collisions and with various beam options, including the use of lead ions with substantial energy. Despite the overwhelming amount of data available, a significant portion remains unexploited, particularly in the 10-100 GeV range, where the majority of existing research focuses on two-body processes or saturated results from heavy-ion collisions. This paper aims to re-examine existing data on hadron-hadron collisions at the LHC, focusing on the production of minor hadron systems and combining relevant searches with constraints derived from heavy-ion collisions, colliders, and laboratory experiments. By re-analyzing these constraints within the context of established theories, we demonstrate how they can be effectively presented for future reference, with an emphasis on equating cross-sections for minor systems to constant values that vary with energy and charge. Furthermore, we introduce a new approach that incorporates the distribution of charge in proton-proton collisions, which may be useful for interpreting collisions at future high-energy experiments. The underlying assumptions and methods are discussed in an appendix for reference purposes. The generated dataset and resulting constraints are available for download. The ongoing production of new data at the LHC will inevitably lead to the inclusion of more restrictive constraints on hadron-hadron collisions, with opportunities for new physics discoveries that could fundamentally transform our understanding, driving the need for an updated analysis in the future. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring patterns of behavior. This study challenges that idea by revealing that the intervals between which neutron star binaries experience outbursts are not random and can be explained by a single distribution that applies across the sample, whether it includes the suspected black hole binaries or not. When taking into consideration the time it takes for these sources to experience outbursts, researchers found that many of the neutron star binaries may have disappeared, consistent with the predicted length of time it takes for a low-mass binary to disappear following its last outburst. This finding provides evidence that the variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade may actually be neutron star binaries rather than black holes. This study based on observations of the known neutron star binary systems V4641 Sgr, XTE J0347-435, and 4U 0345+309 determines the probability that the inactive variables in the Milky Way's center have formed outbursts in the last 10-20 years and find that the probability is quite low. If future observations confirm the absence of outbursts from these sources in the last two decades, it would provide significant evidence for the theory that they are actually black holes. The study also found patterns in the outburst intervals of known neutron star binaries, with sources that have shorter outburst intervals also experiencing shorter intervals between their outbursts, or specific outburst intervals that repeat every 7-10 years. The most persistent of these patterns could help researchers determine the nature of specific variables in the Milky Way's center. Thermodynamics and disorderly motion play a significant role in the functionality and malfunctioning of materials, particularly those with low entropy phases. Despite their significance, the role of thermal motion in the breakdown of these materials has not been thoroughly understood. This study demonstrates the substantial impact that thermal motion can have on the breakdown of these materials by revealing the development of massive barriers to scattering and the disappearance of low entropy phases with increasing temperature. This research was conducted on monolayer copper oxide, a well-known, highly versatile material. However, the findings are expected to be applicable to other materials, including superconducting calcium-doped ruthenium oxide and the pseudogap phase of high-temperature superconductors, after accounting for physical differences. The likely breakdown of these materials can be compared to the collapse of a bridge, where the removal of individual strands may not cause collapse, but the addition of more strands beyond a critical point will lead to its collapse. This research was conducted using theoretical methods, but experimental observation of thermal motion's impact is necessary for a complete comprehension. The likely location of critical points can be identified using energy and temperature measures that indicate the start of collapse, and have been shown to be applicable to the mentioned materials, including others with low entropy phases. The possible ways in which thermal motion affects spin rather than position also have been investigated, showing that it can have an additional detrimental effect on the stability of these materials. The study has implications for the high-fidelity control of low entropy phases and suggests that thermal control of phonons may be as critical as the control of temperature and magnetic fields in this regard. Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with the capability for sustained nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates, rather than slow rotation alone. Using these simulations, we determined the boundaries within which stars could maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning. These boundaries varied based on angular momentum. However, above a certain threshold (approximately 8.85 x 10^48 erg s) the boundaries broke into two distinct branches, resulting from objects losing mass and experiencing extreme spin. This research was applied to model the development of sub-stellar objects. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number. The paper presents an iterative procedure for discovering such a representation, with an associated algorithm having a runtime directly proportional to the number of nodes breaking, in addition to a parameter influencing the performance, which is continually optimized during the process. The approach has further value in facilitating the inclusion of newly discovered relationships in the visualization. We introduce a new category called disentangled links in a certain type of enhanced knot theory, which incorporates classical and welded links. This category allows us to define a meaningful operation called disentanglement for knots. We demonstrate that adding disentanglement as a operation turns the enhanced knot theory into a non-commutative monoid. Furthermore, this operation combines classical and welded knot theories through a forgetful functor. Specifically, it yields the operation of minimal crossing number in classical knot theory and the Bruzzo-Melrose invariant in welded knot theory. We establish that the foregetful functor from disentangled knots to classical knots is an embedding of the braid group within the classical knot theory, utilizing the 4-color theorem. We achieve a similar result for welded knots by establishing that the foregetful functor from disentangled knots to welded knots is an embedding of the braid group. Both of these results can be viewed as extensions of a preceding discovery by Morwen and Kauffman. We also investigate properties of the disentanglement operation, finding that it is compatible with combinatorial laws governing the Kauffman polynomial. Additionally, we determine the impact of the disentanglement operation on various invariants of knots, discovering that it enables the dissemination of distinct knots and verifying that it couples with the arborification invariant. We conclude by analyzing the possibility of spreading or dispersing knots via the disentanglement operation, which leads to the concept of the dispersal matrix. We propose and evaluate several possible definitions of this matrix, which could be utilized to investigate dispersal as a equitable operation or equivalent to equality as a property of knottiness. We determine the dispersal matrix for various types of torus knots and knot projections, and present results on the interconnection between dispersal, arborification, and cross ratios. We also find that the dispersal matrix can be utilized to spread or dissolve the knots of a given type, or to generate or develop new types of knots, or to define a notion of diversity for knots, or to investigate the equitable operation of dispersal on knots, or to determine the equivalence between different types of knots, or to investigate the relationship between knots and graphs, or to investigate the relationship between knots and surfaces. We conclude by presenting a conjecture on the dispersal matrix of torus knots and knot projections, and provide a way of defining the dispersal matrix for a general enhanced knot theory, or a general surface, or a general graph, or a general set of surfaces. Task synchronization in robotics involves coordinating tasks to occur at specific times, which can be critical in applications like cleaning or maintenance schedules. In this research, we focus on strategic multi-task synchronization, where robots can selectively participate in tasks that align with their individual interests. Assuming robots operate in a network with competition for attention and follow other robots, our goal is to determine how they can synchronize tasks effectively. We developed a mathematical model representing this situation and discovered that the robots' ability to follow each other is reduced when the network is highly congested. To enhance task synchronization, we recommend robots prioritize tasks that offer the highest payoff for the greatest amount of time between task completion times. Our study also demonstrates that, in isolated systems, tasks are synchronized at intervals that are perfect powers of two. Furthermore, in larger networks, we found that robots degrade to a sub-perfect power of two dynamic system behavior. Our findings have been validated through computational simulations. This study was featured at the 2022 IEEE Conference on Decision and Control and Systems and Control. Look for an extended version in the IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control under the name "Strategic Multi-Task Synchronization in Robust Networks of Limited Capability Robots". A related commentary can be found in the companion paper "Policy Persistence in Hybrid Systems of Robust Take-Over Requests". A numerical example and simulation code are available online. In order to circumvent these limitations and efficiently process large datasets, this paper introduces an alternative method of kernel estimation that leverages insights specific to the underlying data and offers both a randomized and low-dimensional feature space transformation. In our study, we demonstrated how both a group that operates on a set in a recurring manner and a diagonal group are effectively incorporated into the wreath products under their combined, or product action, utilizing the Cartesian breakdown method. Specifically, we established that any group that operates on a set in a recurring manner and a diagonal group are seamlessly integrated into the wreath products through their combined action in the form of a substructure that resembles a product structure, where the underlying components consist of (1) the wreath products itself, considered with a modified action, and (2) the dual of the original action, operating on the power set of the original set. This research paper examines conformally flat hypersurfaces of n-dimensional space (n is 4 or higher) within a hypersphere of n+2 dimensions. Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $N$-gram models still excel in many situations with low computational costs, demonstrating a strong foundation of language understanding. Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural model that learns from the remaining knowledge between $N$-gram models and the true language distribution, allowing for both a deeper grasp of language and the flexibility to adjust models through the $N$-gram base without altering the neural model. Through extensive experiments on tasks including language modeling, machine translation, and summarization, our hybrid approach consistently delivers enhanced performance over standard neural models and facilitates seamless domain adaptation by simply swapping the $N$-gram base, eliminating the need for additional training. Our code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/NgramRes.

Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. Moreover, our approach achieves simple and broad generalization, demonstrating superior results on more challenging datasets such as the recently launched AFLW2019-3D. Our code has been made publicly available at https://github.com/ghristian/SADRNet.

Researchers examined marked ordered trees with the ability to designate some leaves as "required", denoted as r, and the remaining leaves as "optional", denoted as o. A "deepest" vertex in such marked trees is defined as the farthest vertex from the root that has a higher degree than its children, considering the impact of missing children due to leaves being optional. The study computes the expected number of deepest vertices, accounting for tree structure and the effect of missing children, and determines that the highest degree a deepest vertex can have is always one, meaning the farthest vertex always has a higher degree than its children, including when considering missing children. Therefore, the study equates the number of deepest vertices to the number of branches ending in r. A specific formula is derived for the number of deepest vertices, and various special cases are explored, including trees with a single required leaf, trees with multiple required leaves, uniform trees, binary trees, and trees with a specified number of optional leaves. Additionally, the study provides an integral expression for the number of deepest vertices in randomly generated trees where each leaf has an equal probability of being marked as required or optional. The study also discusses the distribution of the number of deepest vertices in random trees and determines that it follows a negative binomial distribution. The most likely number of deepest vertices in such trees is found to be directly proportional to the square root of the number of optional leaves. The study concludes by examining the relationship between the number of optional leaves and the height of the tree, and it shows that the most likely number of deepest vertices remains constant even when the tree height varies. The study further explores this constant relationship in random uniform trees and finds that the number of deepest vertices remains the same as it is determined by the number of required leaves. The study also discusses the dynamic nature of the number of deepest vertices in marked trees, the change in the number of deepest vertices when a leaf changes from optional to required, or vice versa, and it shows that such a change can result in the number of deepest vertices remaining the same, increasing by one, or becoming non-existent. The study concludes by examining the scenario of such changes in random uniform trees and determines that the number of deepest vertices in such trees remains dynamic, but the number of trees with a specific number of deepest vertices follows a geometric distribution. This investigation seeks to examine whether, via visual recognition, it's possible to determine the origin of a scanned ballot tally. To explore this, we developed a new method, Informed OCR or iOCR, which incorporates a step where the algorithm attempts to distinguish the scanner that generated each scan before applying character recognition. We discovered that iOCR outperforms standard OCR approaches in multiple assessment metrics. Furthermore, our findings indicate that training iOCR on a broad, diverse dataset of scanner scans can lead to increased effectiveness in identifying the source of unknown scans. To demonstrate the practical applications of iOCR, we used it to analyze a large dataset of scanned election ballot totals and developed a method to estimate the frequency of duplication errors based on scan characteristics. This analysis reveals that the frequency of duplication errors varies significantly, from less than 1% to over 60%, depending on the scanner and election district. This research and the iOCR tool can be useful for election officials and other stakeholders who work with scanned documents, particularly in areas where duplication errors pose a significant problem. We open-sourced iOCR on GitHub to facilitate its use and modification by others. In addition, we propose potential improvements to the tool, including integrating machine learning methods to enhance its performance. Lastly, we highlight the limitations of iOCR and identify possible areas for further development, such as developing a more sophisticated method to estimate the frequency of duplication errors and an approach to tackle the issue of scanner change-over, where a scanner is switched from one environment to another but remains undetected by the iOCR system. This would require the development of a more detailed dataset of scanner profiles that can be compared with the iOCR results. This research received no external funding. In recent years, researchers explored a linear model with an overparameterized framework, discovering that overfitting can often be comprehended as a beneficial aspect of training. This phenomenon has been demonstrated to occur in data sets that are randomly generated and in image classification using a neural network. This study extends the overparameterized scenario to linear models involving time series data and shows that non-sparse data learning results in a combination of two distinct phases. During the initial phase, the model absorbs the underlying pattern of the time series, while in the subsequent phase, it enters an overfitting stage where the model becomes overly complex and inaccurate. A mathematical analysis of a first-order optimization method along with numerical examples involving random data and real stock price analysis, are used to illustrate this phenomenon. This study also explores different regularization techniques that influence the overfitting stage and provides an alternative interpretation of the results using a change in the model's underlying pattern. This research offers a specific time series-based example to explain overfitting in an overparameterized framework. This study uses a linear approach, but it also discusses the potential for overfitting in non-linear models, such as neural networks, in time series data contexts. We find that conservative individuals tend to overestimate the benefits of storage and underestimate its costs, leading them to install smaller units. This effect is more pronounced when market volatility increases, causing a significant decline in storage adoption. Our proposed "dynamic learning" technique tackles issues related to large-scale neural network training, particularly on extremely broad classification tasks like ImageNet. We show that initializing the labels for a subset of the dataset is sufficient to successfully train efficient neural networks, without the need for explicit label reduction methods. We demonstrate this approach, which we call "dynamic learning," involves treating uninitialized labels as noise, thereby leveraging their vast quantity to enhance model performance. The key benefit of dynamic learning is the simplicity of its implementation, as it doesn't require any modifications to the optimization algorithm or the network architecture. Furthermore, we find that initializing only 0.4% of the ImageNet labels is sufficient to achieve superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art, with an accuracy of 68.3% on the ILSVRC 2012 dataset. The code for this paper is available at https://github.com/ghrua/dynamic-learning.

Our investigation focused on the conductive properties of HgTe quantum wells near their critical thickness, where the energy gap is minimal, and the energy spectrum is described by a singular Dirac cone structure. Both theoretically and experimentally, we analyzed the thin-film equivalents, focusing on whether they form a two-dimensional equivalent of a graphene sheet or a cylindrical Dirac surface. Our findings showed that in films with a mirror plane along the x-y direction, there's no surface scattering of Dirac electrons, and therefore no 2D Anderson localization or classical percolation of the 2D percolation model. Instead, we observed 1D behavior in films with a single row of HgTe quantum wells along the x, y, or z axis, characterized by 1D localization or percolation of Dirac electrons. This result highlights the unique properties of HgTe quantum wells with a mirror plane and demonstrates that by adjusting the thickness, Dirac electrons can exhibit a range of 1D to 3D conduction behaviors. Furthermore, this suggests that these gapless quantum wells could serve as ideal platforms for implementing 1D or 2D Dirac materials, providing access to a controlled parameter space through layering, without the presence of surface roughness or defects. Additionally, we analyzed the experimental and theoretical conductance data, confirming that in films with a mirror plane along the x-y direction, there's no influence of the 2D Anderson localization or classical percolation of the 2D percolation model. Instead, we found experimental and theoretical conductance matching in films with a mirror plane along the x, y, or z axis, and proposed a method for determining the wave function's symmetry by analyzing the conductance of individual rows of HgTe quantum wells along the x, y, or z axis. Moreover, we examined the effects of misalignment and surface roughness on the conduction properties, finding that even under these conditions, the films exhibit 1D behavior in all directions, and suggesting that in practice, this 1D behavior could be induced by adjusting the thickness of the HgTe quantum wells. Lastly, we proposed a method for generating nanoscale magnetic barriers within the gapless HgTe quantum wells by utilizing a combination of piezoelectric materials and external magnetic fields, providing access to a range of coupled Dirac and magnetic systems. Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves identifying the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically using BERT, have led to significant gains in WSD accuracy by employing a zero-shot or few-shot learning approach.  However, these methods have limitations when applying to words with numerous senses, as they require access to pre-trained models with the target senses.  To address this challenge, we develop a novel framework termed Context-gloss WSD, which leverages gloss context to enhance the word's context and facilitate disambiguation.  This framework is applicable to words with both few and many senses and has been successfully applied to six datasets.  Our results show that it outperforms the baseline BERT-based methods by a 10% average F-score margin in the few-sense case and significantly improves the performance in the many-sense case by achieving the best F-score across six datasets, as compared to other BERT-based methods.  Our study highlights the significance of words' glosses in enhancing context and the versatility of our approach in addressing both few and many senses scenarios.  We also explore two variants of our framework and analyze the impact of selecting glosses on WSD accuracy.  Our code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/Context-gloss-WSD.

Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set J times. The aim is to mitigate performance estimation's intrinsic instability and facilitate effective parameter tuning by prioritizing variance minimization over bias. In line with this principle, our study advocates for a smaller K than typically adopted and instead invests computational resources in increasing the value of J, as demonstrated across diverse NLP tasks including sentiment analysis, part-of-speech tagging and text classification. The resulting models prove significantly more resilient to unstable evaluations and significantly more precise in contrast to conventional k-fold CV. The optimal parameters obtained yield models that not only excel on the standard evaluation set but also demonstrate excellent across-fold consistency and significant improvements over conventional k-fold CV in many cases. The code and data for the experiments reported are available at the website: https://github.com/ghrua/jk-fold-tuning.

When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of fluids undergo shear thickening, a sudden and extreme response characterized by an abrupt transition from fluid-like behavior to solid-like behavior. Despite its surprising consequences, the underlying reasons for shear thickening remain poorly understood, especially in polymer-based suspensions, which can increase in viscosity by as much as millions of times. Until now, research has focused on localized shear thickening, neglecting the effects of shear thickening on the entire system's behavior, particularly in instances where the stress exceeds a certain threshold. In our current study, we investigate the relationship between stress and shear thickening's intensity, demonstrating that shear thickening follows a global scaling law that connects the viscosity's variation to the distance between two relevant disorder or disorder-like states. Our findings are applicable to a wide range of materials and scenarios, ranging from highly congested mixtures of polymers and particles to turbulent flows, and even dusty or sandy fluids like those found in geophysical contexts. Our research reveals the intricate link between stress, disorder, and shear thickening's intensity, offering a novel perspective on this enigmatic phenomenon and providing a framework for predicting the effects of stress on complex systems' behavior. We derive a universal exponent of approximately 2 that defines the geometry of shear thickening's transition, making it possible to extend and refine our scaling law to better fit the unique characteristics of each specific system. Our approach also allows us to identify the stress threshold below which shear thickening fails to manifest or behaves erratically, completing the scaling law and further elucidating the complex relationships between stress, disorder, and shear thickening's intensity. We thoroughly test our derived scaling law using a combination of our own data and previously published results, ranging from the flow of highly congested polymer chains to the shear thickening behavior of flamewalls in the inferno of the 2013 Sacrimonte forest fire. Our analysis of these systems reveals the incredible versatility of our found universal exponent of 2, making it possible to predict the effects of stress on complex systems with a high level of accuracy, and offering a fundamental understanding of the underlying mechanisms governing shear thickening transitions. We further demonstrate the applicability of our scaling law to predict the stress threshold below which shear thickening fails to manifest or behaves erratically, also known as the Narse-Hele-Shaw threshold, which marks the point at which the system's behavior changes from isolated shear thickening to global instability.
